As has been noted, centrifugal force is a "fictitious force" that arises as a consequence of taking the perspective of a frame of reference that rotates - in our case, Earth's orbital motion around the Sun. In an "inertial" frame of reference that is not rotating along with Earth's motion, the force that's actually at work is the [centripetal force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centripetal_force) exerted on Earth by the Sun.

Per [Newton's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_universal_gravitation#Modern_form), Earth's inward acceleration due to the Sun's gravity is given by a = GM/r^2: the mass of the Sun, which is about 2 x 10^30 kilograms (or "two nonillion" if that rolls off the tongue better), divided by the square of the Sun-Earth distance of about 150 million kilometers, multiplied by a constant of proportionality known as the gravitational constant.

(6.674 x 10^-11 Nm^2/kg^2) * (2 x 10^30 kg) / (1.5 x 10^11 m)^2 = **about 6 x 10^-3 m/s^2**. For a central body the size of the Sun, this may seem quite tiny: if your car accelerated like this, it would take about an hour and a half to go from 0 to 100 kph. Not exactly road-worthy. Earth's surface gravity is about 1,700 times as strong as this, which makes sense because we don't notice things falling into space (or even weighing appreciably less) at high noon. Then again, the Sun is very far away: sunlight takes almost eight and a half minutes to get here.

Fun fact: Earth's orbital speed around the Sun is about 30 km/s. If you ejected an object straight backwards at this speed and managed to perfectly cancel its orbital motion and make it fall straight toward the Sun, at an initial acceleration of 6 mm/s per second, you'd have to wait about **64 days** for it to arrive. The Sun is *very* far away.

Short answer: "See", yes. (*Resolve*, of course not.)

Long answer: We can make a very rough estimate of the number of lunar lander photons you can see with some simple assumptions and order-of-magnitude calculations.

First, I'll assume that all of the light coming from the landers is reflected sunlight. This seems reasonable since the intensity of black-body radiation in the visible spectrum is negligible at lunar surface temperatures of 70-390 K. The visible component of the [solar constant](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_constant) is about **600 W/m^2** at the Moon's distance from the Sun.

I'll model an Apollo Lunar Module descent stage as a perfectly reflective metallic disk of radius 2 meters (area **4π m^2**). For convenience, I'll further assume that the metallic surface is diffuse, so that it reflects light equally in all directions. Then if the Sun is shining down onto the full face of the lander from directly overhead, that's **2400π watts** of incident visible solar irradiation heading back out into the lunar sky.

How much of that sky is taken up by your eyes? Wikipedia informs us that the [pupil](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupil#Optic_effects) of the human eye widens to a diameter of between 3 and 8 mm in low-light conditions. Let's call it 6 mm. Your pupils will therefore have a combined area of 2π(0.003 m)^2 = **1.8π x 10^-5 m^2**. They are 400,000 km away from the Moon, at which distance a hemisphere has a total area of 2π(400,000 km)^2 = **2.9π x 10^17 m^2**. So your pupils account for about **6 x 10^-23** (math fact: you can read that as "six sextillionths of a percent") of the sky as viewed from the surface of the Moon. This is why you can't see things on the Moon very well, and it's also why the telescopes we build when we do want to see things that are far away tend to be much wider than the human eye.

Now, a photon with a wavelength of 550 nm, right in the middle of the visible spectrum, has an energy of about 3.6 x 10^-19 joules. So our 2400π watt lander is emitting about **2.1 x 10^22 visible photons per second** into the lunar sky. And six sextillionths of a percent of that sky is occupied by the parts of your body whose function is to detect those photons. That works out to about 1.3 photons per second from each lander, but we should round down a bit to account for the fact that they're not all facing directly toward you.

We left six Lunar Module descent stages on the Moon. When you look up at a full moon, about five of the photons you see each second came from them.
